points.description: Final answer is 11, reached with valid reasoning throughout. The reasoning must contain a lower bound and an upper bound. Lower bound: with at most 10 queries there are at most 2^10 = 1024 < 2021 membership patterns, so two indices lie in exactly the same queried sets and cannot be told apart (the hidden numbers can be arranged so that their roles cannot be separated). Upper bound: 11 queries suffice, since 2^11 - 1 = 2047 >= 2021. Give distinct nonzero 11-bit codes to the indices, query by bit position, and recover each x_i from the answers using pairwise coprimality, for example by gcds or prime factorisation of the answers. Any valid alternative argument for 11 is accepted. Any invalid step or any other final answer earns 0.

rubric.notes: Full mark only if the final answer is 11 and the argument is valid, with both a lower bound (fewer than 11 queries cannot separate 2021 indices) and a construction with 11 queries. A wrong answer, or a lower bound or construction that is invalid, earns 0. There is no part credit.
rubric.answer_key: Answer: 11 queries. Lower bound: with k queries there are 2^k membership patterns for the indices. If k <= 10, then 2^k <= 1024 < 2021, so two indices i and j are in exactly the same queries. Bob then only sees products that treat x_i and x_j symmetrically, so he cannot tell which factor belongs to which index. Hence k >= 11. Upper bound: 2^11 - 1 = 2047 >= 2021, so assign each index a distinct nonzero 11-bit code. Query k is the product of x_i over the indices whose code has bit k set. Because the x_i are pairwise coprime, the prime factors of each x_i appear in exactly the queries given by its code. So each prime's code identifies the index it belongs to, and x_i is the product of the prime powers carrying code i. The minimum is 11.
